questions.title: Increased pain sensitivity in the normal skin surrounding an area of injury is called what?
questions.question: A patch of normal, uninjured skin surrounding a burn becomes painfully sensitive to light touch, even though the burn itself is a short distance away. What is this phenomenon called?

explanations.A: Correct. Secondary hyperalgesia is exaggerated pain sensitivity in normal, uninjured skin surrounding (not within) an area of tissue damage. It results from central sensitisation — increased excitability of dorsal horn neurons receiving convergent input from the surrounding skin — rather than from any direct injury to that skin's own nociceptors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary hyperalgesia is exaggerated pain sensitivity within the injured tissue itself, from peripheral nociceptor sensitisation by locally released inflammatory mediators — not in the surrounding normal skin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Allodynia (pain from a normally non-painful stimulus) can accompany secondary hyperalgesia in the surrounding skin, but the named phenomenon being tested here, exaggerated pain in tissue outside the injury, is specifically secondary hyperalgesia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Referred pain is pain perceived at a site distant from its true (often visceral) origin, due to convergent afferent input — a different mechanism from the local spread of sensitisation around a skin injury.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute increased pain sensitivity in the normal skin surrounding an injury to secondary hyperalgesia (central sensitisation).

questions.title: A sunburned patient feels pain from the light pressure of a jacket. What mechanism explains this?
questions.question: A woman who sunbathed develops a sunburn and, later, feels pain simply from the light pressure of putting on her jacket over the burned skin. Which mechanism best explains this increased pain sensitivity at the site of the burn itself?

options.A: Sensitisation of peripheral nociceptors by locally released inflammatory tissue products
options.B: Central sensitisation of dorsal horn neurons receiving input from unburned skin
options.C: Loss of descending inhibition from the periaqueductal gray
options.D: Increased conduction velocity in A-delta fibres

explanations.A: Correct. This is primary hyperalgesia: chemical mediators released by damaged tissue at the burn site — prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and other inflammatory products — lower the activation threshold of the peripheral nociceptors in that tissue. Because those nociceptors are now sensitised, a previously innocuous stimulus, such as the light pressure of clothing, is perceived as painful. The sensitisation is confined to the injured tissue itself, which is the defining feature of primary (as opposed to secondary) hyperalgesia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes secondary hyperalgesia, which occurs in the normal skin surrounding an injury, not at the injury site itself — the vignette specifically places the pain at the burned skin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Loss of descending inhibitory control would produce a more generalised increase in pain sensitivity, not the localised sensitisation confined to the site of tissue damage described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyperalgesia at an injury site reflects a lowered activation threshold of nociceptors, not a change in axonal conduction velocity.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute primary hyperalgesia at an injury site to peripheral nociceptor sensitisation by locally released inflammatory tissue products.

questions.title: A lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere produces incoordination on which side of the body?
questions.question: A lesion confined to one cerebellar hemisphere produces limb incoordination (ataxia) on which side of the body?

options.A: The same (ipsilateral) side as the lesion
options.B: The opposite (contralateral) side to the lesion
options.D: Neither side; cerebellar lesions do not affect limb coordination

explanations.A: Correct. Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates voluntary movement on its own (ipsilateral) side, because cerebellar efferents cross twice — once leaving the deep cerebellar nuclei toward the contralateral red nucleus/thalamus, and again when the corticospinal tract they influence decussates in the medulla — restoring a net ipsilateral relationship. A unilateral cerebellar lesion therefore produces ataxia and dysmetria on the same side as the lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Contralateral control is the rule for the cerebral motor cortex (single decussation at the pyramids), not the cerebellum, which has a net double decussation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A unilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces lateralised, not bilateral, incoordination — confined to the ipsilateral limbs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cerebellum is central to coordinating the timing, force, and accuracy of voluntary movement; a hemisphere lesion produces clear ipsilateral incoordination (ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor).

questions.learning_objective: State that the cerebellum coordinates ipsilateral limb movement, in contrast to the cerebral cortex's contralateral control.

questions.title: An infarction of the blood vessels supplying the cerebral cortex, involving the primary motor area, produces which pattern of paralysis?
questions.question: An ischaemic infarction involving the blood vessels that supply the primary motor cortex produces which pattern of weakness?

options.C: Contralateral flaccid paralysis with no reflex change

explanations.A: Correct. The primary motor cortex gives rise to corticospinal fibres that decussate at the medullary pyramids in the lower medulla. A lesion of the cortex itself — including ischaemic infarction of the vessels supplying it — produces an upper motor neuron syndrome of spastic paralysis, exaggerated reflexes, and an extensor plantar response on the contralateral side of the body. The weakness is contralateral precisely because the corticospinal fibres cross below the level of the cortical lesion, at the pyramids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The corticospinal tract decussates below the level of a cortical lesion (at the medullary pyramids), so the resulting weakness is contralateral, not ipsilateral, to the lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An upper motor neuron lesion (cortical infarction) produces spastic paralysis with exaggerated, not absent, reflexes; flaccid paralysis with no reflex change is the pattern of a lower motor neuron lesion instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A focal unilateral cortical infarction produces lateralised, contralateral weakness, not bilateral symmetrical weakness.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute contralateral spastic hemiplegia to a lesion (e.g. vascular infarction) of the primary motor cortex.

questions.title: A lesion of the right fasciculus gracilis causes loss of vibration sense in the right tibia. Why the same side?
questions.question: A patient with a lesion confined to the right fasciculus gracilis loses vibration sense over the right tibia, below the level of the lesion. Why is the sensory loss on the same (ipsilateral) side as the lesion, rather than the opposite side?

options.A: Dorsal column fibres ascend uncrossed and decussate only in the lower medulla
options.B: Spinothalamic fibres ascend uncrossed and decussate only in the thalamus
options.C: The fasciculus gracilis crosses at the level of entry, then re-crosses in the medulla
options.D: Vibration sense is represented bilaterally at every spinal level

explanations.A: Correct. Fibres in the fasciculus gracilis (lower limb) and fasciculus cuneatus (upper limb) ascend on the same side of the spinal cord and do not cross the midline until they form internal arcuate fibres in the lower medulla. A unilateral lesion below that decussation therefore produces ipsilateral, not contralateral, loss of vibration and proprioceptive sense.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes the (crossed) spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature and decussates in the spinal cord itself — the opposite pattern to the dorsal columns, and not the pathway carrying vibration sense.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fasciculus gracilis does not cross at the segmental level of entry; it ascends uncrossed the entire length of the spinal cord and crosses only once, in the medulla.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vibration sense in each dorsal column is a unilateral (ipsilateral, pre-decussation) representation, not a bilateral one — this is exactly why a unilateral lesion produces a unilateral (ipsilateral) deficit.

questions.learning_objective: State that a unilateral dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis) lesion causes ipsilateral, not contralateral, loss of vibration sense below the lesion.

questions.title: Which receptor type carries the afferent limb of the flexor withdrawal reflex?
questions.question: The afferent (sensory) limb of the flexor withdrawal reflex, triggered by touching a hot surface, is carried by which receptor type?

explanations.A: Correct. The flexor withdrawal reflex is triggered by a noxious stimulus, and its afferent limb is carried by free nerve endings — the nociceptors that transduce noxious mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli. These afferents synapse on spinal interneurons that excite flexor motor neurons of the stimulated limb, producing withdrawal. The same interneurons also drive, via the crossed extensor reflex, extension of the opposite limb.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Muscle spindles are proprioceptors signalling muscle length/stretch; they are the afferent limb of the (unrelated) stretch reflex, not the nociceptive withdrawal reflex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Golgi tendon organs signal muscle tension and drive the inhibitory autogenic reflex on the same muscle, not the noxious-stimulus-triggered withdrawal reflex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors for vibration, not the nociceptive receptor type that initiates withdrawal.

questions.learning_objective: Identify free nerve endings (nociceptors) as the afferent receptor type for the flexor withdrawal reflex.

questions.title: Why are superficial (e.g. abdominal) reflexes lost in an upper motor neuron lesion, while deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated?
questions.question: In an upper motor neuron lesion, the superficial abdominal reflexes are typically lost, while the deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated. What explains the loss of the superficial reflexes specifically?

options.A: Superficial reflexes depend on an intact corticospinal tract, which the lesion has interrupted
options.B: Superficial reflexes are purely spinal reflexes with no supraspinal input at all
options.C: Superficial reflexes require an intact peripheral nerve, which the lesion has damaged
options.D: Superficial reflexes are mediated by the same circuit as deep tendon reflexes

explanations.A: Correct. Superficial (cutaneous) reflexes such as the abdominal reflex require a functioning corticospinal tract input to the spinal segment, unlike deep tendon reflexes, which do not share this dependency. An upper motor neuron lesion that interrupts the corticospinal tract therefore abolishes the superficial reflexes below the lesion, even as it simultaneously exaggerates the deep tendon reflexes (loss of descending inhibition).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Superficial reflexes are not purely spinal — their preservation specifically requires corticospinal (supraspinal) input, which is exactly why they are lost when that input is interrupted.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An upper motor neuron lesion is central (corticospinal tract), not peripheral; the peripheral nerve carrying the reflex's afferent and efferent limbs is intact.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superficial and deep tendon reflexes are not mediated by the same circuit — that is precisely why an upper motor neuron lesion affects them in opposite directions (superficial reflexes lost, deep reflexes exaggerated).

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the loss of superficial (e.g. abdominal) reflexes in an upper motor neuron lesion to their dependency on an intact corticospinal tract.

questions.title: Which chemical mediator is classically identified as a pain-producing (algesic) substance?
questions.question: Which of the following chemical mediators is classically identified as directly algesic (pain-producing) when released at a site of tissue injury?

explanations.A: Correct. Bradykinin, a kinin generated at sites of tissue injury and inflammation, is one of the most potent directly algesic (pain-producing) chemical mediators. It acts on peripheral nociceptor terminals to trigger pain signalling directly, not merely to sensitise them to other stimuli. It is also a key contributor to the sensitisation underlying hyperalgesia at the injury site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Histamine's principal actions are vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability (contributing to itch more than direct pain), not the primary algesic mediator role that bradykinin plays.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prostaglandin E2 mainly sensitises nociceptors to other stimuli (lowering their threshold) rather than being the classic directly pain-producing mediator itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C5a is chiefly an anaphylatoxin and chemotactic factor for inflammatory cells, not a direct nociceptor-activating pain mediator.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bradykinin (a kinin) as a directly algesic (pain-producing) chemical mediator released at sites of tissue injury.

questions.title: Which receptor is chiefly responsible for detecting vibration?
questions.question: Which mechanoreceptor is chiefly responsible for detecting vibration?

explanations.A: Correct. The Pacinian corpuscle is a large, encapsulated, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor found in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Its onion-like lamellated capsule filters out sustained pressure and selectively tunes it to high-frequency mechanical oscillation. This makes it the receptor chiefly responsible for detecting vibration, distinct from the other cutaneous mechanoreceptors tuned to other modalities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The muscle spindle signals muscle length and the rate of change of length (stretch), not cutaneous vibration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Golgi tendon organ signals muscle tension, not vibration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Merkel discs are slowly adapting receptors for sustained pressure and texture discrimination, not vibration, which requires a rapidly adapting receptor like the Pacinian corpuscle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Pacinian corpuscle as the mechanoreceptor chiefly responsible for detecting vibration.

questions.title: Golgi tendon organ (Ib) afferents ultimately inhibit which neurons, and by what kind of circuit?
questions.question: Golgi tendon organ Ib afferents, signalling increased muscle tension, ultimately inhibit which neurons in the spinal cord, and by what kind of circuit?

options.A: The alpha motor neurons of the same muscle, via a disynaptic circuit through an inhibitory interneuron
options.B: The alpha motor neurons of the same muscle, via a direct monosynaptic synapse
options.C: The alpha motor neurons of the antagonist muscle, via a direct monosynaptic synapse
options.D: The gamma motor neurons of the same muscle only, with no effect on alpha motor neurons

explanations.A: Correct. The Golgi tendon organ's Ib afferents enter the spinal cord and synapse on an inhibitory interneuron. That interneuron, in turn, inhibits the alpha motor neurons supplying the same (homonymous) muscle — a disynaptic circuit, not a direct synapse. The net effect is that excessive tension in a muscle reflexively reduces that same muscle's own contraction, a protective reflex called autogenic (inverse myotatic) inhibition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Golgi tendon organ reflex is disynaptic, routed through an inhibitory interneuron; the monosynaptic reflex arc (direct Ia afferent-to-alpha-motor-neuron synapse) instead describes the stretch reflex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The reflex inhibits the same (homonymous), not the antagonist, muscle's alpha motor neurons — it is an autogenic (self), not a reciprocal, inhibitory reflex.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The tendon organ reflex's principal action is inhibition of the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle; it is not restricted to the gamma motor neurons.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the Golgi tendon organ reflex arc: Ib afferent to an inhibitory interneuron to inhibition of the alpha motor neurons of the same muscle.
